### The Origins and Rise of Rome (753 BCE – 27 BCE)

The history of the Roman Empire begins not with an emperor, but with a myth and a small city-state on the banks of the Tiber River in central Italy. According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BCE by Romulus, who, after killing his twin brother Remus in a dispute over leadership, became the city's first king. While the tale of the she-wolf nursing the twins captures the Roman imagination, archaeological evidence suggests that Rome evolved gradually from a collection of Latin and Sabine villages on the Palatine Hill.

For its first two and a half centuries, Rome was ruled by seven kings, a period known as the Regal Era. These early monarchs, a mix of Latin and Etruscan rulers, laid the foundational infrastructure of the city, including the construction of the Cloaca Maxima (the great sewer) and the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill. However, the monarchy ended in 509 BCE when the last king, Tarquin the Proud, was expelled following a revolt sparked by the tyranny of his family and the rape of Lucretia, a noblewoman. This event marked the birth of the **Roman Republic**.

The Republic was defined by a complex system of checks and balances designed to prevent the return of tyranny. Power was vested in two annually elected consuls, the Senate (an advisory body of aristocrats), and various popular assemblies. During the next four centuries, Rome transformed from a regional power into a Mediterranean hegemon. Through a series of grueling conflicts, most notably the three Punic Wars against Carthage (264–146 BCE), Rome secured dominance over the western Mediterranean.
